Text: An adult human skeleton has {{c1::206::number of bones}} bones.
Back Extra:
Why: a newborn has around 270 separate bony pieces, and many fuse as you grow (pieces of single skull bones, the hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx), which is how the adult count settles at 206.

Pitfall: the lab manual counts 210 because it adds two sesamoid bones in each foot; the BIOL 214 lab itself uses 206.

Text:
Sort each bone into its division of the skeleton:

auditory ossicles → {{c1::axial::axial or appendicular}}

hyoid → {{c1::axial::axial or appendicular}}

sacrum → {{c1::axial::axial or appendicular}}

hip bone (os coxae) → {{c1::appendicular::axial or appendicular}}
Back Extra:
Why: the axial skeleton is the body's central pole (skull with its ear bones and hyoid, thoracic cage, and vertebral column down through the sacrum and coccyx), while the appendicular skeleton is the limbs plus the girdles that hang them from that pole.

Pitfall: the sacrum sits between the two hip bones but belongs to the spine, so it is axial; the hip bones form the pelvic girdle, so they are appendicular.

Text: Bones are classified by shape into five classes: {{c1::flat}}, {{c1::long}}, {{c1::short}}, {{c1::sesamoid}}, and {{c1::irregular}}.
Back Extra:
Why: shape follows job: long bones are levers, short bones pack into blocks, flat bones are shields, sesamoids sit in tendons, and irregular bones fit an odd job.

Mnemonic: Five Lazy Skeletons Sit Idle = Flat, Long, Short, Sesamoid, Irregular.

Text: The sphenoid, ethmoid, maxilla, mandible, zygomatic, and inferior nasal concha are {{c1::irregular::shape class}} bones.
Back Extra:
Why: bones such as the sphenoid, ethmoid, and maxilla wrap around the eyes, nose, sinuses, and teeth, so each has an odd 3-D shape (wings, plates, sockets, air spaces) that fits no simpler class.

Pitfall: not every skull bone is flat. The curved plates of the braincase (such as the frontal, parietal, and occipital) are flat, but complex bones like the sphenoid, ethmoid, maxilla, and mandible are irregular.

Text: Bone markings are divided into two landmark categories: {{c1::projections}} and {{c1::depressions}}.
Back Extra: Why: a bone's surface is shaped by what touches it. Muscles and ligaments raise projections where they anchor, joints use both (a rounded head or condyle fitting a socket-like fossa), and vessels and nerves leave depressions such as grooves and foramina.

Text: The shaft of a long bone is the {{c1::diaphysis}}, and each knobby end is an {{c2::epiphysis}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the diaphysis is a hollow tube of compact bone that makes a strong, light lever, while the wider epiphyses spread the load where the bone meets its neighbor at a joint.

Parts: dia- (between) + -physis (growth); epi- (upon) + -physis. The diaphysis grows between the ends, and the epiphyses sit upon the shaft.

Cue: one diaphysis, but two epiphyses (proximal and distal).

Text: A long bone grows in length at its {{c1::epiphyseal plate}}, and it is the {{c2::diaphysis::which part}} that lengthens.
Back Extra:
Why: the plate is a band of cartilage between the shaft and the end whose cells keep dividing, pushing the epiphysis away while bone fills in behind them.

Meaning: the epiphyseal plate is also called the growth plate.

Text: Inside the epiphyseal plate, new cartilage is added on the {{c1::epiphysis::epiphysis or diaphysis}} side, while bone is added on the {{c1::diaphysis::epiphysis or diaphysis}} side.
Back Extra:
Why: the plate grows at its outer edge while being turned into bone at its inner edge, so it creeps outward, pushing the end of the bone away and lengthening the shaft.

Pitfall: the lab words the same fact as cartilage growth on the distal end of the plate while bone is added medially, so distal = the epiphysis side and medial = the diaphysis side.

Text: When growth is complete, the epiphyseal plate becomes the {{c1::epiphyseal line}}.
Back Extra: Why: once its cartilage stops dividing, bone replaces the whole plate, and the thin bony line left behind is the scar of the old growth plate.

Text: The epiphyseal plate is made of {{c1::cartilage::bone or cartilage}}, while the epiphyseal line is made of {{c1::bone::bone or cartilage}}.
Back Extra:
Why: cartilage can keep growing from within, so a cartilage plate can lengthen the bone; once the plate turns to bone (the line), lengthening is over.

Distinguish: the plate (cartilage) marks where growth is still happening; the line (bone) marks that growth has ended.

Pitfall: growth happens at the plate, never at the line.

Text: The most abundant cartilage in the body is {{c1::hyaline::cartilage type}} cartilage, and the least abundant is {{c1::elastic::cartilage type}} cartilage.
Back Extra: Why: hyaline is used wherever a smooth, slightly flexible surface is needed (most joint surfaces, the rib cartilages, the trachea, the nose), while elastic is needed only in the few places where tissue must bend and spring back.

Text: The most flexible cartilage is {{c1::elastic::cartilage type}} cartilage, found in the {{c2::external ear}} and the {{c2::epiglottis}}.
Back Extra: Why: elastic cartilage's matrix is threaded with elastic fibers, so it bends and snaps back into shape. Fold your ear and it springs right back.

Text: Hyaline cartilage is {{c2::flexible::stiff or flexible}} and covers the {{c1::articulating surfaces::where on the bone}} of bones.
Back Extra: Why: hyaline cartilage's glassy-smooth surface cuts friction where two bones meet, and because it covers the articulating (joint) surface, it is also called articular cartilage.

Text: Of the three cartilages, {{c1::fibrocartilage}} is the stiffest and toughest, which lets it {{c2::absorb force::what it does}} in the {{c3::intervertebral discs}} and the knee's {{c3::menisci}}.
Back Extra: Why: thick bundles of collagen fibers run through its matrix, so it resists squeezing and tearing, the right material for a shock absorber.
